Rx: topical steroids, systemic steroids with or without azathioprine, methotrexate, or dapsone. Refer to ophthalmology.

problems.description: Deep pocket adjacent to a tooth whose pulp has died — or a periapical lesion on a tooth with deep pocketing — where the two lesions have merged and it is unclear which came first.
problems.etiology: A combined lesion is where both periodontal and pulpal lesions coalesce, regardless of which started first [1]. The primary periodontal route: progressive periodontitis eventually reaches the apex. The primary endodontic route: pulp necrosis causes periapical pathology that then involves the periodontal tissues [1]. In fact, there is little evidence to support the popular notion that periodontitis leads to pulp necrosis — but pulp pathology can exacerbate periodontal problems [1]. Sensibility testing is essential before assuming the diagnosis is purely periodontal [2].
problems.presentation: A heavily restored tooth with deep pocketing, or a tooth with known periodontitis that develops a periapical radiolucency, or a tooth that fails to respond as expected after periodontal treatment alone. The patient may have symptoms of both — throbbing pain and a sinus — alongside pocket depth findings.
problems.results: Sensibility test the tooth — non-vitality in a tooth with a deep pocket points strongly toward a pulpal component [2]. Full-mouth periapical radiographs will show both the lateral bone loss of periodontal disease and the periapical radiolucency of pulpal pathology [3]. The diagnostic challenge is that both conditions look similar on radiograph and probe similarly.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Here's the practical rule: treat the endodontic component first and wait. The apparent periodontal lesion will often resolve substantially over a period of months — so defer the decision about surgery [4]. The worst prognosis applies to teeth where periapical/pulpal pathology is entirely due to apical extension of the periodontal pocket — these are often diagnosed retrospectively when endodontics fails to resolve the lesion [4].
problems.treatment: First: resolve the acute infection and inflammation by drainage and/or antibiotics [4]. Then: orthograde RCT — the greater the pulpal component, the better the prognosis [4]. Re-assess the periodontal element at 3–6 months. Combined apical surgery and periodontal surgery is feasible but carries a poorer long-term prognosis [4].
problems.prognosis: The greater the pulpal component, the better the prognosis after endodontic treatment [4]. Teeth where the primary driver is apical extension of a deep periodontal pocket have the worst outlook [4].

citations.quote: A combined periodontal–endodontic lesion is where both lesions coalesce regardless of whether the origin is primarily periodontal (necrotic pulp due to periodontal involvement) or primarily endodontic (periodontal tissues involved after pulp necrosis). Given the relative frequency of both periodontal disease and periapical pathology, it is not surprising that both may occur together, which can result in diagnostic confusion. In fact, there is little evidence to support the popular notion that periodontitis leads to pulp necrosis. However, there is no doubt that pulp pathology can exacerbate periodontal problems.
It is essential to sensibility test any heavily restored tooth with periodontal involvement.

Full mouth periapicals (preferably of the long cone parallel technique), have been the radiographs of choice for patients with severe periodontal disease. They can clearly demonstrate root surface deposits, furcation involvement, extensive bone loss, intrabony pocketing, and periodontal–endodontic lesions.

First, resolve the acute infection and inflammation by drainage (&/or antibiotics), then treat with orthograde RCT (the greater the pulpal component, the better the prognosis). The apparent periodontal lesion will often be seen to resolve to a substantial degree over a period of months, therefore, the decision to carry out surgery should be deferred. Combined apical surgery and periodontal surgery is quite feasible but carries a poorer long-term prognosis. The worst prognosis applies to those teeth where the periapical/pulpal pathology has been due entirely to apical extension of the periodontal pocket. These are often diagnosed after the fact, when endodontics completely fails to resolve the lesion.

problems.description: Red, fleshy, easily bleeding lump on the gum — soft, vascular, arising after repeated minor trauma or irritation.
problems.etiology: A response to recurrent trauma and non-specific infection [1]. Histology shows proliferation of vascular connective tissue, which is why it bleeds so easily [1].
problems.presentation: A red fleshy swelling, often nodular, on the gingiva or elsewhere in the mouth. Bleeds readily on minimal contact [1]. The patient often notices it is growing slowly or bleeds when they eat or brush.
problems.results: Biopsy and histology confirm the diagnosis — proliferation of vascular connective tissue is the characteristic finding [1]. Vitality testing of adjacent teeth is positive; this is not an endodontic or bony lesion.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining feature is the bright red, easily-bled, vascular, often nodular surface [1]. In pregnant patients an identical lesion is called a pregnancy epulis — histologically and clinically indistinguishable from pyogenic granuloma [2]. So always ask about pregnancy when you encounter this picture.
problems.treatment: Excise, debride the area, and establish good oral hygiene [1].
problems.prognosis: Good after excision with adequate debridement. Recurrence is possible if the local irritant is not removed.

citations.quote: A red fleshy swelling, often nodular, occurring as a response to recurrent trauma and non-specific infection. Histology shows proliferation of vascular connective tissue, therefore it bleeds easily. Rx: excision, debride area, and good OH.
An ↑ inflammatory response to plaque during pregnancy causes a lesion indistinguishable from a pyogenic granuloma.

problems.description: A soft, bleeding gum lump appearing in the third month of pregnancy — clinically identical to a pyogenic granuloma.
problems.etiology: An increased inflammatory response to plaque during pregnancy causes a lesion indistinguishable from a pyogenic granuloma [1]. Onset is usually in the third month [1].
problems.presentation: A soft, vascular, readily-bleeding gum swelling in a pregnant patient. Usually anterior. Onset in the first trimester, growing through pregnancy [1].
problems.results: Biopsy shows the same vascular connective tissue proliferation as a pyogenic granuloma. The pregnancy history and timing are the distinguishing context.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The pregnancy epulis is histologically and clinically indistinguishable from a pyogenic granuloma [1]. What marks it out is the context: the patient is pregnant, onset was around the third month, and — here's the key for treatment decisions — it will regress after delivery [1].
problems.treatment: None other than oral hygiene instruction if at all possible, as it regresses after delivery [1]. If very troublesome, simple excision is performed — but warn the patient it may recur during the pregnancy [1].
problems.prognosis: Regresses after delivery [1]. Excision during pregnancy is effective but recurrence before delivery is possible [1].

citations.quote: An ↑ inflammatory response to plaque during pregnancy causes a lesion indistinguishable from a pyogenic granuloma. Onset usually in third month. Rx: none (other than OHI) if possible, as it regresses after delivery. If very troublesome, simple excision is performed; but it may recur.

problems.description: A deep red, firm gingival swelling — the classic 'giant cell epulis' — probably arising from chronic local irritation.
problems.etiology: Probably caused by chronic irritation [1]. The exact trigger is a local irritant — a calculus deposit, a rough restoration margin, a denture flange.
problems.presentation: A deep red gingival swelling. Often firm on palpation. May be sessile or pedunculated. Bleeds readily [1].
problems.results: Histology is the definitive test: a vascular lesion with multinuclear giant cells [1]. Radiograph should be taken to check for underlying bone involvement.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The deep red colour and the multinuclear giant cell histology are the defining features [1]. The interesting bit is that treatment requires more than simple excision — stripping of the periosteum and curettage of the underlying bone are necessary to reduce recurrence [1].
problems.treatment: Excision with stripping of the periosteum and curettage of underlying bone [1].
problems.prognosis: Good after adequate excision with periosteal stripping and bone curettage. Recurrence is possible if the periosteum is not addressed.

citations.quote: (Giant cell epulis.) This is a deep red gingival swelling, probably caused by chronic irritation. Histology reveals a vascular lesion with multinuclear giant cells. Rx: excision with stripping of periosteum and curettage of underlying bone.

problems.description: A soft lump on the gum present from birth — pedunculated, present at birth, granular cells on biopsy.
problems.etiology: By definition present at birth [1]. The source does not specify a cause beyond this.
problems.presentation: Usually presents as a pedunculated nodule on the gingiva at birth [1].
problems.results: Histology reveals large granular cells — this is the defining histological finding [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: What makes this distinctive is its presence at birth and its characteristic large granular cell histology [1]. The granular cell content distinguishes it histologically from other neonatal gingival lesions.
problems.treatment: Complete but conservative excision [1].
problems.prognosis: Good after complete conservative excision [1].

citations.quote: By definition, this is present at birth; it usually presents as a pedunculated nodule. Histology reveals large granular cells. Rx: complete but conservative excision.

problems.description: Spontaneous gingival bleeding, gingival swelling, and petechiae in a patient with a haematological malignancy — not explained by local periodontal disease alone.
problems.etiology: Leukaemia and other haematological malignancies are associated with a decreased resistance to infection and with haematological changes affecting platelet function and coagulation [1]. The gingival swelling in leukaemia is partly infiltration of the gingival tissues by leukaemic cells and partly the secondary inflammatory response driven by reduced immune surveillance [1].
problems.presentation: Bleeding and petechial haemorrhage even with minimal trauma, gingival swelling, ulceration, and mucosal pallor [1]. Candidosis and herpetic infections may be superimposed because of reduced resistance to infection [1]. Spontaneous gingival bleeding may occur even without probing.
problems.results: A blood picture distinguishes this from severe plaque-induced gingivitis. The gingival swelling is different in character — it may be diffuse, covering the crowns, and does not respond to plaque removal in the way that plaque-induced gingivitis does.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The interesting bit is that the gingival signs here are a systemic disease manifesting locally — not a primary periodontal condition. The diagnosis of leukaemia-associated gingivitis comes from the medical history and blood results, not from probing alone [1]. Gingivitis associated with blood dyscrasias is listed as a distinct category in the periodontal classification [2].
problems.treatment: Prevention of superinfection: chlorhexidine mouthwashes [1]. Aggressive appropriate treatment of infections that arise [1]. Management of bleeding is aimed at the underlying disorder; local techniques include improving OH, avoiding extractions, and using local haemostatic methods [1]. Spontaneous gingival bleeding may be controlled using impressions as a made-to-measure pressure dressing [1].
problems.prognosis: Depends on the underlying haematological malignancy and its treatment. Local measures reduce secondary infection risk but do not alter the primary disease course [1].

citations.quote: This and other haematological malignancies are associated with a ↓ in resistance to infection leading to candidosis or herpetic infections. Other oral problems include bleeding and petechial haemorrhage (even with minimal trauma), gingival swelling, ulceration, and mucosal pallor. Prevention of superinfection with chlorhexidine mouthwashes and aggressive appropriate Rx of infections which arise are of real help. Management of the bleeding is aimed at the underlying disorder; local techniques include improving OH, avoiding extractions, and using local haemostatic methods. Spontaneous gingival bleeding may be controlled by using impressions as a made-to-measure pressure dressing.
Gingivitis associated with blood dyscrasias, e.g. leukaemia-associated gingivitis.

problems.description: Recurrent bouts of oral ulceration, acute periodontal flares, or NUG-like episodes in a regular 3–4-week cycle.
problems.etiology: A genetic condition characterised by cyclic neutrophil suppression. The periodic collapse of neutrophil numbers leaves the periodontium and oral mucosa vulnerable to infection in predictable 3–4-week cycles [1].
problems.presentation: Oral ulceration, acute exacerbations of periodontal disease, or NUG, recurring in 3–4-week cycles [1]. The cyclical pattern is the diagnostic clue.
problems.results: Serial blood counts at different points in the cycle will demonstrate the neutrophil nadir. The periodontium may look near-normal between cycles, then deteriorate acutely during the neutropenic phase.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The rule of thumb here is the cycle: 3–4 weeks, predictably recurring [1]. Any patient with recurrent NUG or acute periodontal flares that clear spontaneously and then recur should prompt consideration of cyclical neutropenia. NUG in an apparently healthy person can also signal HIV, but the cyclical pattern is specific to this condition [1].
problems.treatment: Address acute episodes with local debridement and chlorhexidine as for NUG. The systemic management of cyclical neutropenia is medical — liaise with haematology.
problems.prognosis: The oral manifestations mirror the neutrophil cycle. Without systemic control of the neutropenia, recurrence is inevitable [1].

citations.quote: This condition may manifest as oral ulceration, acute exacerbations of periodontal disease, or NUG. As the name suggests, it recurs in 3–4-week cycles.

problems.description: An unusually intense red band along the gingival margin, out of proportion to the amount of plaque, in a patient with HIV.
problems.etiology: Strongly associated with HIV infection [1]. The characteristic feature is an intense red band at the gingival margin that is unusually severe relative to the oral hygiene status — the normal plaque-response relationship breaks down because of immune suppression [1].
problems.presentation: Unusually severe gingivitis for relatively good oral hygiene. Often characterised by linear gingival erythema — an intense red band along the gingival margin [1]. The severity of the gingival inflammation is disproportionate to the plaque load.
problems.results: Probing reveals the inflamed margin but pocketing may be shallow. The key finding is the intense erythema relative to plaque scores. HIV status should be established or reconsidered in a patient presenting with this picture.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The mismatch is the tell: intense red band at the margin with a relatively clean mouth [1]. In the HIV oral manifestation classification, this is a Group I condition — strongly associated with HIV [1].
problems.treatment: Plaque control and local debridement. Chlorhexidine mouthwash as adjunct. Address HIV status with the patient's medical team.
problems.prognosis: Response to conventional periodontal therapy may be limited while immune suppression persists. With antiretroviral control of HIV, gingival status may improve.

citations.quote: Unusually severe gingivitis for relatively good OH. Often characterized by linear gingival erythema, an intense red band along the gingival margin.

problems.description: Severe, localised periodontal destruction out of all proportion to plaque levels — in a young, otherwise apparently healthy patient with HIV.
problems.etiology: Strongly associated with HIV [1]. Immune suppression allows rapid, localised periodontal destruction that is disproportionate to plaque loads — the same immune-mediated mechanism that drives linear gingival erythema but extending into the deep tissues.
problems.presentation: Severe localised destruction out of place with oral hygiene status [1]. Rapid bone and attachment loss in a patient who may have only moderate plaque.
problems.results: Probing reveals deep pockets and clinical attachment loss. Radiographs show bone destruction. The degree of destruction is the clue — it does not match the plaque scores.
problems.definingCharacteristics: What separates HIV periodontitis from aggressive periodontitis is the HIV context and, often, the association with other HIV oral signs — candidosis, hairy leucoplakia, linear gingival erythema [1]. Severe localised destruction in an apparently healthy young person is a prompt to consider HIV status.
problems.treatment: Non-surgical periodontal debridement. Plaque control. Chlorhexidine. Address the underlying HIV with the patient's medical team.
problems.prognosis: With antiretroviral therapy improving immune function, periodontal status may stabilise. Without immune control, progression continues.

citations.quote: Severe localized destruction out of place with OH.

problems.description: Gums that have slowly grown over the teeth since childhood — dense, fibrous, painless overgrowth with no drug history.
problems.etiology: A lesion of genetic origin [1]. In contrast to drug-induced gingival overgrowth, there is no medication responsible — this is an intrinsic connective tissue hyperplasia with a genetic basis [1].
problems.presentation: Dense, fibrous gingival overgrowth. Slow onset from childhood. Pale, firm tissue. May cover substantial portions of the crown. Painless.
problems.results: Drug history is negative for phenytoin, ciclosporin, and calcium channel blockers — this is the key finding that separates hereditary fibromatosis from drug-induced overgrowth [1]. Histology shows dense fibrous connective tissue.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The clinical appearance is identical to drug-induced gingival overgrowth — firm, pale, fibrous enlargement beginning interdentally and spreading to cover the crown [1]. What distinguishes hereditary gingival fibromatosis is the absence of any causative drug and the genetic pattern, often with a positive family history. No drug history: that single fact changes the diagnosis.
problems.treatment: Gingivectomy for significant overgrowth affecting function, aesthetics, or plaque control. Unlike drug-induced overgrowth, there is no drug to change — recurrence after surgery is common.
problems.prognosis: The overgrowth tends to recur after gingivectomy. Long-term management requires repeated surgery in severe cases.

citations.quote: These include gingival lesions of specific bacterial, viral, or fungal origin, lesions of genetic origin (e.g. hereditary gingival fibromatosis), gingival manifestations of systemic conditions (mucocutaneous disorders, allergic reactions), traumatic lesions, and foreign body reactions.

problems.description: Gingival disease driven by vitamin C deficiency — bleeding, swollen, spongy gums in a patient with poor diet.
problems.etiology: Caused by ascorbic acid (vitamin C) deficiency — classified under gingival disease modified by malnutrition [1].
problems.presentation: Bleeding, swollen, spongy gingiva in the context of a diet grossly deficient in vitamin C. The gingival changes will not resolve with plaque control alone while the deficiency persists.
problems.results: The medical and dietary history is the key investigation. Serum vitamin C levels confirm the deficiency. Gingival findings overlap with plaque-induced gingivitis but respond differently to treatment.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining point is that the gingivitis is driven by malnutrition rather than by plaque alone [1]. Plaque removal alone will not resolve scurvy gingivitis while vitamin C remains deficient. This is a rare diagnosis in UK practice but should be considered in patients with very poor diet, alcohol dependence, or limited food access.
problems.treatment: Vitamin C supplementation to correct the deficiency. Plaque control and PMPR alongside.
problems.prognosis: Resolves with vitamin C replacement and plaque control once the nutritional deficiency is corrected.

citations.quote: Gingival disease modified by malnutrition. These would include ascorbic acid-deficiency gingivitis (scurvy) and gingivitis due to protein deficiency.

problems.description: Gums that bleed more than expected in a teenager with reasonable plaque control — the gingival inflammation exaggerated out of proportion to the local cause.
problems.etiology: There is a well-recognised increase in the severity and frequency of gingivitis at puberty [1]. This is listed in the periodontal classification as a distinct subcategory — endocrine-modified gingivitis — under gingival disease modified by systemic factors [2].
problems.presentation: Gingivitis in an adolescent that is more severe than would be predicted by the plaque score. The usual signs of plaque-induced gingivitis — red, swollen, bleeding gums — are present but magnified.
problems.results: BPE and plaque scores as for gingivitis. The clue is that the severity of the gingival response is disproportionate to the plaque load. No bone loss; no attachment loss.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Puberty gingivitis is real, but it is still plaque-dependent — it does not occur in the absence of plaque [1][2]. The thing is, the exaggerated response is hormonally mediated, but the treatment is still plaque control. Without effective plaque removal it won't resolve, regardless of the hormonal modifier.
problems.treatment: Thorough OHI. Professional plaque removal. Reduce plaque load — the hormonal modifier amplifies the response to existing plaque, so plaque removal is still the cure.
problems.prognosis: Improves naturally as hormone levels stabilise after puberty, provided plaque control is established. Neglected puberty gingivitis in susceptible individuals can progress to periodontitis.

citations.quote: There is a well-recognized ↑ in the severity and frequency of gingivitis at puberty and in pregnancy.
Endocrine system: puberty-associated gingivitis, menstrual cycle-associated gingivitis, pregnancy-associated gingivitis, pyogenic granuloma, diabetes mellitus-associated gingivitis.

problems.description: Severe early-onset periodontal disease and fragile, easily-bruised gums in a patient with hyperextensible joints and skin — a connective tissue condition with distinct dental implications.
problems.etiology: A rare inherited connective tissue disease characterised by hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, and fragile vessels due to mutations in collagen [1]. Oral features include severe early-onset periodontal disease [1]. Bleeding during surgery, weak scars, and sutures pulling through are the main practical issues [1]. Bleeding is commoner in type IV; early-onset periodontal disease in type VIII [2].
problems.presentation: Severe periodontal disease at an unusually early age, in the context of easy bruising and bleeding of the skin and oral mucosa [1]. The patient may have very mobile joints. Small teeth with short roots and pulp stones may be noted on radiograph [1].
problems.results: Probing reveals periodontal disease disproportionate to the patient's age. Radiograph may show short roots [1]. Pulp stones visible on periapical films [2]. The connective tissue diagnosis is usually already known; if not, the combination of early periodontitis, fragile tissue, and hypermobility should prompt medical investigation.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The periodontal destruction here is driven by the collagen defect in the PDL and supporting tissues, not primarily by plaque [1]. The interesting bit for surgical planning: sutures pull through, scars are weak, and vessels are fragile — these practical complications make periodontal surgery in this group hazardous [1]. Some types carry increased susceptibility to infective endocarditis and cerebrovascular risk from vessel weakness [1].
problems.treatment: Treatment is aimed at the symptoms [1]. Non-surgical periodontal therapy first. If surgery is necessary, anticipate wound dehiscence and fragile tissue [1]. Liaise with the patient's medical team regarding endocarditis prophylaxis if valve involvement is known [1].
problems.prognosis: Periodontal disease tends to be early-onset and severe because of the underlying collagen abnormality [1][2]. Conservative management and meticulous plaque control are the priority; surgery carries significant healing complications.

citations.quote: A rare inherited connective tissue disease characterized by hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, and fragile vessels due to mutations in collagen. This results in very easy bruising and bleeding of skin as well as oral mucosa. Oral features include severe early-onset periodontal disease, small teeth with short roots, pulp stones, and occasional hypermobility of the TMJ. Bleeding during surgery, weak scars, sutures 'pulling through', and difficulty with root canal Rx are the main practical points. Some types of Ehlers–Danlos syndrome can lead to an ↑ susceptibility to infective endocarditis and significant heart damage due to mitral valve prolapse, and some types are prone to cerebrovascular accident due to weakness of intracranial blood vessels. Rx: aimed at the symptoms.

A group of disorders characterized by hyperflexibility of joints, ↑ bleeding and bruising, and hyperextensible skin. There appears to be an underlying molecular abnormality of collagen in this inherited disorder. Bleeding is commoner in type IV, early-onset periodontal disease in type VIII. Pulp stones may be seen in all types.

problems.description: Severe gingivitis, periodontitis, and aphthae in a young child, combined with abnormal skin pigmentation and a history of recurrent infections.
problems.etiology: A genetic disease combining defective neutrophil function with abnormal skin pigmentation, resulting in increased susceptibility to infection [1]. The neutrophil defect removes the first-line defence against periodontal pathogens, leading to severe periodontal disease even in young children [1].
problems.presentation: Severe gingivitis, periodontitis, and aphthae in young children [1]. Abnormal skin pigmentation is the systemic clue. Recurrent infections are the broader pattern [1].
problems.results: The combination of severe periodontal disease at a very early age with systemic immune deficiency and skin changes should prompt investigation. Blood count will show the neutrophil abnormality.
problems.definingCharacteristics: What makes this distinguishable is the triad: defective neutrophil function, abnormal skin pigmentation, and increased susceptibility to infection — all in a child with severe gingivitis and periodontitis [1]. The periodontal disease here is a direct consequence of the neutrophil defect.
problems.treatment: Periodontal debridement and plaque control. Management of the systemic condition is medical. Antimicrobial adjuncts may be needed during acute phases.
problems.prognosis: Severe and early-onset. The prognosis for the periodontium depends on control of the systemic immune deficiency [1].

citations.quote: A combination of defective neutrophil function, abnormal skin pigmentation, and ↑ susceptibility to infection (→ severe gingivitis, periodontitis, and aphthae in young children). It is a genetic disease.

problems.description: An aggressive gingivitis and periodontitis that begins at puberty and affects both the primary and secondary dentition — in a child with thickened, scaly skin on the palms and soles.
problems.etiology: Characterised by palmoplantar hyperkeratosis (thickening and scaling of the skin on the palms and soles) combined with juvenile periodontitis that affects both dentitions [1]. Normal dental development occurs until the hyperkeratosis appears on the palms and soles — then simultaneously an aggressive gingivitis and periodontitis begin [1]. The mechanism is not well understood [1].
problems.presentation: Aggressive gingivitis and periodontitis beginning at puberty, affecting both primary and secondary dentition [1]. The palmoplantar hyperkeratosis is the systemic tell — scaly, thickened skin on the palms and soles that appears around the same time as the periodontal disease [1].
problems.results: Radiographs show severe bone loss in both dentitions at an early age. The combination of dermatological and periodontal findings is diagnostic [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The timing is the key: normal development until the skin changes on the palms and soles appear, then periodontal disease begins simultaneously [1]. No other condition in this origin presents with palmoplantar hyperkeratosis as the associated dermatological feature.
problems.treatment: Aggressive periodontal debridement and plaque control. Early extraction of primary teeth affected by severe periodontitis may be considered to protect the secondary dentition. Liaise with dermatology.
problems.prognosis: Without intervention, affected teeth are typically lost early in both dentitions. The condition persists through life.

citations.quote: Palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and juvenile periodontitis, which affects both 1° and 2° dentition. Normal dental development occurs until the appearance of the hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles, then simultaneously an aggressive gingivitis and periodontitis begin. The mechanism is not well understood.

problems.description: Prolonged bleeding from an extraction socket — well beyond the usual hour — in a patient with a platelet or clotting factor disorder.
problems.etiology: Platelet disorders and coagulation defects are the two main categories [1][2]. Platelet disorders include immune thrombocytopenic purpura, Von Willebrand's disease, and thrombocytopenia secondary to leukaemia, cytotoxic drugs, or drug effects — aspirin being the most common acquired cause, with an irreversible effect for one week [1]. Coagulation defects include the haemophilias, anticoagulant therapy, liver disease, and Von Willebrand's disease [2].
problems.presentation: Post-extraction bleeding that persists well beyond normal haemostasis. May also present as nosebleeds, purpura, or spontaneous oral bleeding [1]. The patient may have a known diagnosis, or this event may be the first presentation of an undiagnosed disorder.
problems.results: For platelet disorders: ensure platelet levels >50 × 10⁹/L, preferably 75 × 10⁹/L for anything beyond a simple extraction or LA [1]. A blood coagulation screen identifies clotting factor deficiencies. The haemophilias present as prolonged wound bleeding and/or haemarthroses [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The rule of thumb: haemophilias and Von Willebrand's disease should always be managed at specialist centres — check the patient's warning card for the contact telephone number [3]. Aspirin's irreversible platelet effect lasting one week is the most common acquired cause and the most preventable [1].
problems.treatment: If actively bleeding: combination of local measures, tranexamic acid, and platelet transfusion [1]. Platelet transfusions are short-lived and if used prophylactically must be given immediately prior to or during surgery [1]. Tranexamic acid mouthwash may reduce oral bleeding [1]. Haemophilia and Von Willebrand's disease: manage at specialist haemophilia centres [3].
problems.prognosis: With appropriate management at a specialist centre and correct pre-operative preparation, extraction and other procedures can be safely performed. The risk is in inadequate pre-operative assessment.

citations.quote: May present as nosebleeds, purpura, or post-extraction bleeding. Remember that aspirin is the most common acquired cause, its effect being irreversible for 1 week. Other causes include diseases such as Von Willebrand's disease; immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); virally associated (especially HIV) thrombocytopenic purpura; thrombocytopenia 2° to leukaemia; cytotoxic drugs; or unwanted effects of drugs, notably aspirin and chloramphenicol. Management: ensure platelet levels of >50 × 109/L, preferably 75 × 109/L for anything more than simple extraction or LA. If actively bleeding, use a combination of local measures, tranexamic acid, and platelet transfusion. Platelet transfusions are short-lived and if used prophylactically must be given immediately prior to or during surgery. Tranexamic acid mouthwash may ↓ oral bleeding.
Present as prolonged wound bleeding &/or haemarthroses. Causes include the haemophilias, anticoagulants, liver disease, and von Willebrand's disease.
The haemophilias and Von Willebrand's disease should always be managed at specialist centres. Check the patient's warning card for the contact telephone number.

problems.description: Palatal petechiae or spontaneous gingival bruising in a patient with very low platelet count — often a child.
problems.etiology: Purpura is due to platelet deficiency [1]. The commonest form is idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in children [1]. With too few platelets, minor trauma causes haemorrhage into the mucosa rather than normal haemostasis.
problems.presentation: Palatal petechiae or bruising [1]. Gingival bleeding out of proportion to plaque levels. The palatal petechiae pattern is not specific to ITP alone — it is also seen in glandular fever, rubella, HIV, and recurrent vomiting [1].
problems.results: Blood count shows thrombocytopenia. The diagnosis is established medically. Oral examination shows petechiae on the palate and possibly gingival bleeding.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Palatal petechiae are the telling oral sign [1]. The takeaway for the GDP: palatal petechiae should always prompt a medical history and consideration of whether a blood count is warranted — they are not an isolated dental finding. Multiple causes share this sign, so the broader clinical picture matters [1].
problems.treatment: Management is aimed at the underlying disorder — medical, not primarily dental. Local haemostatic techniques for dental procedures. Avoid extractions unless platelet count is adequate; liaise with haematology.
problems.prognosis: ITP in children often resolves spontaneously. The prognosis for the oral findings follows the platelet count.

citations.quote: Purpura is due to platelet deficiency. Commonest as idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in children. Palatal petechiae or bruising may be seen. Palatal petechiae are also seen in glandular fever, rubella, HIV, and recurrent vomiting.

problems.description: Severe periodontal disease in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes — an infection risk disproportionate to the local plaque picture.
problems.etiology: No specific oral changes in well-controlled diabetes [1]. However, when diabetes is poorly controlled, manifestations of decreased resistance to infection can be seen — severe periodontal disease being the most prominent [1]. Xerostomia and oral thrush are prominent features in ketoacidosis [1]. There is a tendency to slower healing following surgery [1].
problems.presentation: Severe periodontal disease in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes [1]. Xerostomia and thrush in patients in ketoacidosis [1]. Burning mouth may be a presenting feature, and oral or facial dysaesthesia may reflect peripheral neuropathy [1]. Sialosis is sometimes seen as a late feature [1].
problems.results: Periodontal staging and grading as for standard periodontitis — but here the Grade C trajectory (rapid progression) should prompt asking about diabetes. Blood glucose check is part of the medical assessment for unexplained severe or rapidly progressive periodontitis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The thing is, diabetes is a two-way relationship with periodontitis — poorly controlled diabetes worsens periodontal disease, and severe periodontal disease makes glycaemic control harder [1]. Poorly controlled diabetes is one of the two primary risk modifiers in the 2017 periodontal classification. Severe periodontal disease can be the presenting sign of undiagnosed diabetes.
problems.treatment: Periodontal debridement (Steps 1–2 of the BSP pathway). Risk factor control: liaise with the patient's GP about glycaemic management [1]. Slower healing should be anticipated post-surgery [1]. Treat thrush and xerostomia if present [1].
problems.prognosis: Improving glycaemic control improves the periodontal response to treatment. Lichenoid reactions due to oral hypoglycaemic drugs may complicate the mucosal picture [1].

citations.quote: No specific oral changes, although manifestations of ↓ resistance to infection can be seen if poorly controlled (e.g. severe periodontal disease). Xerostomia and thrush are prominent features of ketoacidosis. Sialosis is sometimes seen as a late feature of diabetes. Burning mouth may be a presenting feature, and oral or facial dysaesthesia may reflect the peripheral neuropathies seen in diabetics. There is a tendency to slower healing following surgery. Lichenoid reactions due to oral hypoglycaemic drugs may be seen.

problems.description: Gums that bleed and swell more during pregnancy or at puberty than the plaque load would explain — a hormonally amplified gingival response.
problems.etiology: There is a well-recognised increase in the severity and frequency of gingivitis at puberty and in pregnancy [1]. Some females have recurrent aphthae clearly associated with the menstrual cycle [1]. During the menopause, burning tongue or mouth or general soreness of the tongue or mouth have been described — though these may reflect psychological changes at this time of life rather than a direct hormonal effect, and hormone replacement does not seem to help [1].
problems.presentation: Exaggerated gingivitis relative to plaque levels at puberty or during pregnancy. In pregnancy, the gingival response to plaque is amplified — the patient may have managed their plaque well before but now presents with significant bleeding and swelling [1]. Recurrent aphthae timed to the menstrual cycle in some women [1].
problems.results: BPE findings as for gingivitis — bleeding on probing, no pocketing, no bone loss. The critical finding is that the severity of gingival response is disproportionate to the plaque load. Timing of the condition relative to hormonal events confirms the link.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Hormone-modified gingivitis is still plaque-dependent — it does not arise without plaque [1]. The hormonal change amplifies the inflammatory response but does not initiate it. So the treatment is still plaque removal, but the clinical picture can be dramatic in pregnancy or puberty. Puberty-associated and pregnancy-associated gingivitis are listed as distinct subcategories in the periodontal classification [2].
problems.treatment: Thorough OHI and professional plaque removal. Emphasise that the increased gingival response is temporary and hormone-related, but that plaque control is still necessary to keep it manageable. Pregnancy epulis (pyogenic granuloma) may need simple excision if troublesome — see separate entry.
problems.prognosis: Resolves as hormone levels normalise — after delivery or after puberty — provided plaque control is established [1]. Neglected hormone-modified gingivitis can progress to true periodontitis in susceptible individuals.

citations.quote: There is a well-recognized ↑ in the severity and frequency of gingivitis at puberty and in pregnancy. Some females have recurrent aphthae clearly associated with their menstrual cycle, and several symptoms, usually burning tongue or mouth or general soreness of the tongue or mouth, have been described during the menopause. It should be remembered, however, that there are profound psychological changes at this time of life in many women, and these symptoms may be a manifestation of atypical facial pain rather than a direct hormonally mediated effect. Hormone replacement does not seem to help.
Endocrine system: puberty-associated gingivitis, menstrual cycle-associated gingivitis, pregnancy-associated gingivitis, pyogenic granuloma, diabetes mellitus-associated gingivitis.
